questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I have a faster laptop, I would edit videos more often.
If I had a faster laptop, I would edit videos more often.
If I had a faster laptop, I will edit videos more often.
If I would have a faster laptop, I would edit videos more often.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb: 'If I had a faster laptop, I would edit videos more often.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If he had backed up his files, he wouldn't have lost the data.
If he backed up his files, he wouldn't have lost the data.
If he had backed up his files, he wouldn't lose the data.
If he would have backed up his files, he wouldn't have lost the data.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If he had backed up..., he wouldn't have lost...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This app uses by millions of people worldwide.
This app is using by millions of people worldwide.
This app use by millions of people worldwide.
This app is used by millions of people worldwide.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle: 'is used by millions of people.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The website was hacked last week.
The website hacked last week.
The website was hack last week.
The website is hacked last week.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: 'was hacked last week.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The engineer, who designed this app, used to work at a startup but.
The engineer whom designed this app used to work at a startup.
The engineer which designed this app used to work at a startup.
The engineer who designed this app used to work at a startup.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person: 'The engineer who designed this app...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My phone which I bought last year, still works perfectly.
My phone, that I bought last year, still works perfectly.
My phone which I bought last year still works perfectly but.
My phone, which I bought last year, still works perfectly.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use commas and 'which' for things: 'My phone, which I bought last year, still works perfectly.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: That can't to be a real notification, I never subscribed to that.
That cann't be a real notification, I never subscribed to that.
That can't be a real notification, I never subscribed to that.
That can't being a real notification, I never subscribed to that.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' + base verb expresses a confident negative deduction: 'that can't be a real notification.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The server coulds be down right now.
The server could be down right now.
The server could being down right now.
The server could to be down right now.
questions.explanation: 'Could' + base verb expresses a possible deduction: 'the server could be down.'

questions.topic: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've been sending ten emails this morning.
I've sent ten emails this morning.
I'm sending ten emails this morning already.
I've send ten emails this morning.
questions.explanation: Present perfect simple is used for a completed number of results: 'I've sent ten emails.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've coded since six hours.
I'm coding for six hours already.
I've been coding for six hours.
I've been code for six hours.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an unfinished action: 'I've been coding... for six hours.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I have updated the software.")
options: He said that he has updated the software.
He said that he had updated the software.
He said that he updated the software already.
He said he have updated the software.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect shifts back to past perfect: 'he had updated the software.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "Which browser do you use?")
options: She asked me which browser did I use.
She asked me which browser do I use.
She asked me which browser I use.
She asked me which browser I used.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order (no auxiliary inversion) and shift the tense back: 'she asked me which browser I used.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I used to write letters before emails became common.
I use to write letters before emails became common.
I was used to write letters before emails became common.
I used to writing letters before emails became common.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'I used to write letters before emails became common.'

questions.topic: Be used to / get used to
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I use to typing on a small keyboard now.
I'm used to type on a small keyboard now.
I'm used typing to on a small keyboard now.
I'm used to typing on a small keyboard now.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund: 'I'm used to typing on a small keyboard.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: You need to log in before you can post a comment.
You need to log before you can in post a comment.
You need to log the app in before you can post a comment.
You need to log in to before you can post a comment.
questions.explanation: 'Log in' means 'sign into an account or system': 'log in before you can post.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Always back your files up to before updating the system.
Always back up your files before updating the system.
Always back up to your files before updating the system.
Always back your files before up updating the system.
questions.explanation: 'Back up' means 'make a copy of data for safety': 'back up your files.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Although the slow connection, we finished the video call.
Despite the slow connection, we finished the video call.
Despite of the slow connection, we finished the video call.
Despite the connection was slow, we finished the video call.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (no 'of'): 'Despite the slow connection, we finished the video call.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The server crashed as a result, we lost all our data.
As a result the server crashed we lost all our data.
The server crashed, as a result we lost all our data.
The server crashed. As a result, we lost all our data.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'The server crashed. As a result, we lost all our data.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We don't have enough storage to save the file.
We don't have storage enough to save the file.
We don't have enough of storage to save the file.
We hasn't enough storage to save the file.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes before the noun it modifies: 'enough storage.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My cousin is really good in coding.
My cousin is really good for coding.
My cousin is really good at coding.
My cousin is really good to coding.
questions.explanation: 'Good at' + noun/gerund means 'skilled at something': 'good at coding.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to a tech support team you haven't contacted before?
options: Hey guys,
Yo,
Dear Sir or Madam,
What's up,
questions.explanation: 'Dear Sir or Madam,' is a suitable formal opening when the recipient's exact name is unknown.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email to a named IT manager?
options: Cheers,
Best regards,
Later,
Talk soon,
questions.explanation: 'Best regards,' is a suitable semi-formal closing when writing to a named professional contact.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I wonder if you fix could my account.
I was wondering if you could fix my account.
I was wondering could you fixing my account.
I was wondering if you could to fix my account.
questions.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could' + base verb is a polite way to make a request: 'if you could fix my account.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the developer.' and 'The developer's app went viral.'?
options: This is the developer's app who went viral.
This is the developer which app went viral.
This is the developer who app went viral.
This is the developer whose app went viral.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: 'the developer whose app went viral.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Never I have seen such a fast connection before.
I have never seen such a fast connection before.
I have seen never such a fast connection before.
I have seen such a fast connection never before.
questions.explanation: 'Never' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle: 'I have never seen such a connection.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: I'd like to know whether has the update been installed?
I'd like to know whether the update has been installed.
I'd like to know, whether the update has been installed.
I'd like to know whether the update has been installed?
questions.explanation: Reported/indirect statements use normal word order and end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: This time tomorrow, I ___ a new app.
options: test
will test
will be testing
am testing
questions.explanation: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time: 'will be testing'.

questions.question: By next year, the company ___ a new platform.
options: will have launched
will launch
launches
is launching
questions.explanation: Future perfect describes an action completed before a future point: 'will have launched'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses discourse markers.
options: Secondly firstly back up data, finally install update.
Firstly, back up your data. Secondly, install the update. Finally, restart the device.
Finally back up the data, firstly install, secondly restart device.
Firstly we back data secondly install finally restart.
questions.explanation: Discourse markers 'Firstly,', 'Secondly,' and 'Finally,' organize points clearly with commas.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You wouldn't delete the file, wouldn't you?
You wouldn't delete the file, do you?
You wouldn't delete the file, will you?
You wouldn't delete the file, would you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement with 'would' + positive tag: 'you wouldn't delete..., would you?'
